blocks.text: Mark, a third-year student, decides to 'sort his life out' on 1 January: up at 5 a.m., a daily gym session, cooking every meal, and no social media. By 14 January he has abandoned all of it and feels like a failure. His goals were admirable and unrealistic. Resilience is built less from heroic resolutions than from small habits that survive a bad week.

blocks.markdown: Resilience is the capacity to adapt to stress, setbacks and demanding work without being overwhelmed, and to recover afterwards. It is not a fixed personality trait and it is not the same as 'toughing it out'. It is built from **habits** (sleep, activity and relationships), from **help-seeking** when something is wrong, and from **reflection and peer support** that help us make sense of difficult experiences. This unit covers how to plan realistic habits, the professional duty to seek help for health concerns, and how reflective practice and peer support strengthen resilience.

blocks.title: Resilience
blocks.text: **Resilience** is the ability to adapt and recover in the face of adversity, trauma or significant stress. In medicine it is shaped by individual habits and by the environment: supportive teams, reasonable workloads and a culture in which it is normal to ask for help.

blocks.markdown:
### Planning realistic habits

Three foundations matter for most people: **sleep**, **physical activity** and **social connection**. The aim is not perfection but a plan you can maintain during exams and clinical placements, including night shifts and busy weeks. Plans work better when they are **specific** ('Walk 20 minutes after lunch on Monday, Wednesday and Friday'), **small enough to be easy**, attached to an existing routine ('after I brush my teeth'), and written with a **fallback** for bad days (a shorter version rather than nothing).

blocks.caption: Foundations of resilience and realistic targets
rows: Sleep
Most adults need about 7 to 9 hours; regular timing helps; poor sleep impairs concentration, mood and clinical performance
Fixed wake-up time; screens off 30 minutes before bed; protect sleep after night shifts and plan naps and light exposure
Physical activity
UK Chief Medical Officers' guidelines for adults: at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity a week (or 75 minutes of vigorous), plus muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days
Walk or cycle part of the commute, three 30-minute sessions, stairs instead of lifts
Social connection
Strong relationships protect against stress and loneliness; connection needs time that is scheduled
Weekly meal with friends or family, a call to a relative, a sport or society, a study group
Rest and recovery
Time off from study and work prevents accumulating strain
A protected evening each week, a hobby unrelated to medicine
Substances
Alcohol and caffeine used to cope can worsen sleep and mood
Alcohol-free days, caffeine cut-off time

blocks.title: Building a realistic weekly plan
blocks.prompt: A fourth-year student has a placement with early starts and revision for an exam. They currently sleep 5 hours on weekdays, do no exercise and see friends only when someone organises it. Draft a realistic plan using small, specific changes.

steps.text: Sleep: do not aim for 9 hours at once. Choose a fixed alarm time and move bedtime earlier by 30 minutes this week; screens away 30 minutes before bed. Review progress next week.

Exercise: aim towards 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, but start with something that fits, such as 20 minutes of brisk walking on three days, built into the journey to placement. Increase gradually.
Social connection: schedule one fixed commitment, such as a weekly meal with a flatmate or a sport society on Wednesday, in the diary like a teaching session.
Fallback: write what to do on a bad day, for example a 10-minute walk or a short call instead of skipping entirely.
Review after two weeks: keep what works, adapt what does not, and tell a friend or tutor so someone can check in.

blocks.answer: A good plan has a small number of specific, scheduled and gradually increased habits, with fallbacks and a planned review.

blocks.title: Habits beat heroics
blocks.text: Consistent small habits, planned for bad weeks as well as good ones, protect wellbeing far better than ambitious plans that collapse after a fortnight.

blocks.caption: Help-seeking: barriers and responses
rows: 'I might be judged or damage my career'
Seeking help appropriately is seen as responsible; many services are confidential
Use confidential routes such as your own GP or university support
'I do not have time'
Untreated problems cost more time later and may affect patient safety
Book a short appointment now and plan around it
'I should be able to cope'
Needing help is common and not a sign of weakness
Treat yourself as you would advise a patient
'I can treat myself or ask a colleague'
Self-treatment and informal corridor advice are discouraged by professional guidance
Register with a GP and attend as a patient
'It is not serious enough'
Early help works best and is easiest
Talk to a tutor, GP or wellbeing service early

blocks.title: Applying the duty to seek help
blocks.prompt: A final-year student has had two episodes of near-fainting on placement over the last month, once while standing in theatre. She has not told anyone, hoping it was due to long hours. She has been taking an over-the-counter remedy from a friend for dizziness. Decide what she should do.

steps.text: Identify the risk: recurrent near-fainting can put herself and patients at risk, for example during procedures or while standing in theatre.
Identify the professional duty: she should not self-assess or self-treat, and should seek appropriate medical advice rather than informal remedies.
Action: book an appointment with her own GP promptly, describe the episodes honestly, and follow the advice, including any investigations.

Tell a suitable person about any restrictions that affect safe participation, such as the placement supervisor or occupational health, as advised by her GP or school, so that adjustments can be arranged.
Follow up: review the outcome, and keep appropriate people informed as advised.

blocks.answer: She should see her own GP promptly, avoid self-treatment, follow advice and inform the appropriate people so that any needed adjustments protect her and patients.

blocks.markdown:
### Reflective practice and peer support

**Reflective practice** (see the unit on learning from placement) helps resilience by turning distressing or confusing events into understanding and a plan. Writing or talking through an event, naming your feelings, and asking what you learned reduces rumination and strengthens a sense of control. In the UK, reflection is expected of all doctors, and reflective notes can be kept in a portfolio, with patient details anonymised.

**Peer support** means the structured and informal support colleagues give each other. Examples include buddy or mentor schemes, 'near-peer' support from senior students, post-event debriefs, Balint-style groups (small facilitated groups discussing emotionally demanding clinical cases), and informal check-ins after difficult shifts. Peer support normalises difficulty, offers practical advice and makes it easier to ask for more help. It complements, and does not replace, professional services.

items: Plan small, specific, scheduled habits for sleep, activity and connection, with a fallback for bad days.
Register with your own GP, use them when unwell, and do not self-treat.
Seek advice early if a health problem might affect patient safety and follow the advice given.
After a difficult event, reflect in writing or discussion and use a peer debrief or mentor.
Offer support to colleagues and make it normal to ask for help.

blocks.title: Link the three parts
blocks.text: In an answer about resilience, connect habits (prevention), help-seeking (early treatment when problems occur) and reflection with peer support (processing and sharing difficulty). Examiners reward answers that show how they fit together and relate them to patient safety.

points: Resilience is built by realistic, specific and scheduled habits for sleep (about 7 to 9 hours), activity (at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week for adults) and social connection, with fallbacks for bad days.
Doctors and students have a professional duty to look after their health: register with a GP, seek and follow advice, do not self-treat, and act early if health could affect patient safety.
Reflective practice and peer support help to process difficult experiences, reduce isolation and make help-seeking normal.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of a realistic habit plan?

options.text: Walk for 20 minutes after lunch on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, with a 10-minute walk as a fallback on busy days
Exercise for two hours every day starting tomorrow
Sleep better from now on
Cut out all social activities until finals are over

questions.correctOptionText: Walk for 20 minutes after lunch on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, with a 10-minute walk as a fallback on busy days

distractorRationale.a: Correct: specific, scheduled, achievable and has a fallback.

questions.explanation: Plans that are specific, small and scheduled, with a fallback for difficult days, are more likely to be sustained. Overly ambitious or vague plans tend to collapse.

questions.stem: Which statement best matches UK Chief Medical Officers' physical activity guidance for adults?

options.text: At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days
Ten minutes of activity once a week is enough
Only vigorous activity counts
Activity is only recommended for people with a medical condition

questions.correctOptionText: At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days

distractorRationale.c: Moderate activity counts towards the target.
distractorRationale.d: Activity is recommended for all adults.

questions.explanation: UK guidance recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity weekly, or an equivalent amount of vigorous activity, together with muscle-strengthening on two days. Smaller amounts still bring benefit.

questions.stem: A newly qualified doctor has had troubling chest symptoms for a fortnight and is considering prescribing herself a medicine and asking a friendly consultant to look at her in the corridor. According to professional guidance, what should she do?

options.text: Register with and see her own GP, and follow their advice rather than self-treating or relying on informal corridor consultations
Prescribe herself the medicine to avoid wasting time
Ignore the symptoms until they interfere with work
Wait until her annual leave to think about it

questions.correctOptionText: Register with and see her own GP, and follow their advice rather than self-treating or relying on informal corridor consultations

distractorRationale.a: Correct: professional guidance expects doctors to have their own GP and to avoid self-treatment.
distractorRationale.b: Self-prescribing is discouraged and risks missing serious illness.
distractorRationale.c: Delaying may harm her and patients.

questions.explanation: Doctors should be registered with their own GP and seek independent assessment, because self-treatment and informal advice are prone to bias and missed diagnoses. Chest symptoms in particular need prompt proper assessment.

questions.stem: A student says, 'If I tell anyone I am struggling, I will be reported and thrown off the course.' Which response is most accurate and helpful?

options.text: Seeking appropriate help is regarded as responsible; concealing a problem that affects patient safety is what creates risk, and many services are confidential
She is right, so she should avoid asking for help
All problems will be reported immediately to the regulator
Help should be sought only after failing an exam

questions.correctOptionText: Seeking appropriate help is regarded as responsible; concealing a problem that affects patient safety is what creates risk, and many services are confidential

distractorRationale.a: Correct: help-seeking is encouraged and confidentiality is the norm, with safety exceptions.
distractorRationale.b: Avoiding help is the unsafe option.
distractorRationale.c: Seeking help does not automatically trigger reporting.
distractorRationale.d: Early help is best; waiting for failure is harmful.

questions.explanation: Professional guidance encourages early help-seeking, and fitness to practise concerns arise mainly when significant problems affecting safety are concealed. Confidential services exist so that students can talk freely.

questions.stem: A group of students meets monthly with a facilitator to discuss emotionally demanding patient encounters on placement. Which resilience-building approach does this most closely resemble?

options.text: A Balint-style reflective peer support group
A formal disciplinary hearing
Independent revision for finals
A research ethics committee

questions.correctOptionText: A Balint-style reflective peer support group

distractorRationale.a: Correct: facilitated group discussion of emotionally demanding cases.
distractorRationale.b: A disciplinary hearing is not supportive reflection.
distractorRationale.c: Solo revision is not peer support.

questions.explanation: Balint-style groups bring clinicians or students together to explore the emotional side of clinical encounters. They normalise difficulty and reduce isolation, which strengthens resilience.

questions.stem: True or false: reflective practice means recording only the clinical facts of a case, without mentioning feelings.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Good reflection includes thoughts and feelings as well as facts, because acknowledging emotions helps to make sense of an event and to learn from it. Patient details should still be anonymised.

questions.stem: A student plans three walks of 25 minutes and two cycling sessions of 30 minutes each week, all at moderate intensity. By how many minutes does this fall short of the 150-minute weekly guideline?
questions.explanation: The total is 3 x 25 + 2 x 30 = 75 + 60 = 135 minutes per week. The guideline is 150 minutes, so the shortfall is 150 - 135 = 15 minutes, which could be closed by extending a session or adding a short walk.

questions.stem: A student goes to bed at 23:45 and wakes at 06:30 the next morning, assuming they fall asleep immediately. How many hours of sleep opportunity is this?
questions.explanation: From 23:45 to midnight is 0.25 h and from midnight to 06:30 is 6.5 h, totalling 6.75 hours. This is below the 7 to 9 hours recommended for most adults, so moving bedtime earlier would help.

questions.stem: Describe how you would plan realistic habits for sleep, exercise and social connection during a demanding placement block that includes night shifts.
markingGuide: Sleep: protect a regular routine where possible, plan sleep around night shifts including a wind-down, dark room and avoiding caffeine late in the shift, aiming for 7 to 9 hours over 24 hours
Exercise: small, specific, scheduled sessions towards 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, building activity into travel
Social connection: schedule contact with friends or family and protect at least one social commitment
Habit design: small, specific, tied to routines, with fallbacks for bad days
Gradual progression and review, adapting to what works
Avoiding reliance on alcohol or caffeine to cope
questions.explanation: A practical plan acknowledges the constraints of shift work and uses small, scheduled habits rather than ambitious goals. Including fallbacks and review makes the plan resilient to bad weeks.

questions.stem: Explain the professional duty of doctors and medical students to seek help for their own health concerns, and discuss why people may delay seeking help and how to overcome these barriers.
markingGuide: Duty: be registered with a GP, seek and follow advice from a suitably qualified colleague, avoid self-diagnosis and self-treatment
Reason: impaired health may affect judgement and patient safety
Act to protect patients, for example adjusted duties or time off where advised
Barriers: fear of judgement or career consequences, lack of time, feeling one should cope, stigma, self-treatment habits
Responses: confidential routes such as own GP, tutors, wellbeing services and occupational health; early help works best
Notes that seeking help appropriately is responsible and that concealing a risk to patients is what causes harm
questions.explanation: The duty is grounded in patient safety and in the fact that clinicians are poor judges of their own health. Addressing common barriers shows understanding of why the duty is hard to follow in practice.

questions.stem: Explain how reflective practice and peer support each contribute to resilience, giving an example of each.
markingGuide: Reflective practice: turns difficult experiences into understanding and a plan; reduces rumination and builds a sense of control
Example of reflection such as a written reflection after a difficult encounter using a model, with anonymised patient details
Peer support: shared experience, practical advice and reduced isolation
Example of peer support such as a buddy or mentor scheme, a debrief or a Balint-style group
Both normalise difficulty and make asking for help easier
Peer support complements but does not replace professional help, and confidentiality should be respected
questions.explanation: Reflection builds insight within the individual, while peer support builds connection between people, and both reduce the sense that difficulty is a personal failing. Naming a concrete example of each demonstrates understanding.
